**Reconnaissance on the rollback half, from the installed wrangler rather than from the docs.**

Cloudflare's docs are unreachable from an agent session — the proxy returns 403 on `developers.cloudflare.com`, and that is a policy boundary, not an obstacle to route around. But the installed `wrangler` is authoritative about its own CLI surface, and running `--help` on it is a real run. What that says:

**Workers has a rollback command.**

```
wrangler deployments list [--name <worker>] [--json]   # the 10 most recent deployments
wrangler deployments status                            # the current state of production
wrangler rollback [version-id] --name <worker> -m "<reason>" -y
wrangler versions list                                 # the 10 most recent versions
```

`--json` on `deployments list` is what makes the "record the previous good deploy" step mechanical rather than a screen-scrape.

**Pages has no rollback command.** Its full deployment surface is `list`, `create`, `tail`, `delete` — there is nothing that promotes a previous deployment. So the Pages half is not a wrangler command at all, and whatever it is (the dashboard's own control, or re-deploying the previous build) has to be established by somebody with the account.

**What this does and does not settle.** It settles which commands exist and how they are spelled. It settles nothing about what they *do* — no account exists to run them against (#27), so `wrangler rollback` has never been executed here, and the repo should not carry a rollback procedure written from a `--help` output. Writing down a recovery path nobody has walked is how a 2am command turns out to need a flag it did not have.

So this issue stays open on the same two pieces, now with the first one costed:

- **Record the previous deploy.** One step, `wrangler deployments list --json`, before the deploy step. Cheap to write, impossible to test here — it fails on the missing token before it parses anything.
- **Establish and write down the actual rollback**, both halves, exercised once by someone with the account. Workers looks like one command; Pages looks like it is not a command.

Still deliberately not automated: a smoke failure should stay loud rather than silently reverting.

Refs #27

I went looking for what was left and found that the repo had stopped describing itself accurately. Two merges. **[PR #57](https://github.com/missingbulb/hitbut/pull/57) — the raw bucket's layout, in one place** (`87a7301`, [#56](https://github.com/missingbulb/hitbut/issues/56)). Two local functions both called `rawKeyFor` were building keys into the same R2 bucket in different shapes. Both shapes are right — the crawl re-reads pages that change so it keeps every fetch; the archive keeps one object per document so a retried step *finds* it. What was wrong is that one fact lived in two places under one name, and the consequence went unsaid: **the two namespaces never meet**, so a backfill re-fetches what the crawl already has. Now stated instead of discovered. Proved byte-identical across 108 keys, and I watched that proof fail first. Also corrected three claims that had stopped being true — queue consumers as API writers, a cluster label that "is regenerated" (nothing regenerates it), and the banner still calling the legal review outstanding. **[PR #59](https://github.com/missingbulb/hitbut/pull/59) — a defect that would have cost you time** (`fae2229`, [#58](https://github.com/missingbulb/hitbut/issues/58)). `preflight.ts` listed `queue hitbut-analysis` as a **required** resource. That's the tool [#27](https://github.com/missingbulb/hitbut/issues/27)'s human runs to find out what to create — it would have reported MISS and sent you to provision a queue nothing binds. Ran preflight before and after to watch it leave the checklist. Six more places described the retired shape; the backend README was claiming three modules and an `analysis` that doesn't exist.
**`src/backend/`** — new `raw-keys.ts` owns both key shapes and why they differ; both call sites point at it. **`src/backend/api/`** — the router's header names one writer. **`dev/tools/`** — preflight no longer requires the queue; the Vectorize note names what actually blocks it. **`docs/architecture/`** — the R2 bullet, the API's writers, and what a cluster label really is. **`dev/requirements/`** — the honest-gaps banner (four gaps, not five) and §5's intro.
Three issues also now say what's true: [#28](https://github.com/missingbulb/hitbut/issues/28) rewritten to four open gaps with the legal one recorded as done, [#33](https://github.com/missingbulb/hitbut/issues/33) retitled — its pairing premise was dissolved by #53, and what survives is that **nothing names a cluster**, so every subject chip is empty, and [#36](https://github.com/missingbulb/hitbut/issues/36) now carries what the installed wrangler says about rollback: Workers has `wrangler rollback`, **Pages has no rollback command at all**. I didn't write that into the repo — Cloudflare's docs are 403 from here and I've never run either command, so a 2am recovery path written off a `--help` output is exactly the kind nobody should trust. [#39](https://github.com/missingbulb/hitbut/issues/39#issuecomment-5383994477)'s bisect list is at fifteen. input.body:
With Actions working again, the first green run surfaced a warning on every job:

> Node.js 20 is deprecated. The following actions target Node.js 20 but are being forced to run on Node.js 24: `actions/checkout@v4`, `actions/setup-node@v4`.

The runners are already forcing Node 24, so the actions are running on a runtime they were not built for. When the force ends, they stop.

**Which version actually fixes it**, read from each action's own `action.yml` at the tag rather than assumed:

| action | v4 | v5 | v6 |
|---|---|---|---|
| `actions/checkout` | node20 | **node24** | node24 |
| `actions/setup-node` | node20 | **node24** | node24 |
| `actions/upload-artifact` | node20 | node20 | **node24** |

`upload-artifact` is the trap: v5 is still Node 20, so the obvious "bump everything to v5" leaves that one warning in place — and it sits on the `if: failure()` path, where it would only bite on a day something else is already wrong.

**In scope here**: `product.yml`, `preflight.yml`, `claudinite-ci.yml` — hitbut's own, and none has a stub in the mount, so nothing re-vendors over them. `checkout` and `setup-node` go to v5, matching what the vendored workflows in this repo already use; `upload-artifact` goes to v6 because v5 would not fix it.

**Not in scope, and a gap to carry upstream**: `claudinite-scheduler.yml` and `claudinite-executor.yml` are vendored from the canon's stubs. They are already on `checkout@v5`/`setup-node@v5`, but all three of their `actions/github-script@v7` steps are Node 20 — `github-script@v8` is the Node 24 one. That belongs in Claudinite, not here.

CI works again, and the first green run put a warning on every job: `actions/checkout@v4` and `actions/setup-node@v4` target Node 20 and are being **forced** onto Node 24. That force is temporary — this is a deadline, not noise.

**Which version fixes it**, read from each action's own `action.yml` at the tag rather than assumed:

| action | v4 | v5 | v6 |
|---|---|---|---|
| `actions/checkout` | node20 | **node24** | node24 |
| `actions/setup-node` | node20 | **node24** | node24 |
| `actions/upload-artifact` | node20 | node20 | **node24** |

`upload-artifact` is why that table exists. Its v5 is *still Node 20*, so the obvious "bump everything to v5" would have left the warning on the one step that only runs when a screen golden has already failed — the worst place to discover it. It goes to v6, and the reason sits on the line, because the next person's instinct will be to make it match its neighbours.

`checkout` and `setup-node` go to v5 rather than v6: v5 is the lowest major that fixes the cause, and it is what the vendored Claudinite workflows in this repo already use.

**Untouched:** `claudinite-scheduler.yml` and `claudinite-executor.yml` are vendored from the canon's stubs, and editing them here would be overwritten. They are already on v5 — but their three `actions/github-script@v7` steps are Node 20, and `@v8` is the Node 24 one. That is a gap for Claudinite, noted in #65.

## Verification

This PR's own CI run is the verification: the same three workflows, exercised on a `pull_request` trigger. A tag that did not resolve would fail the job outright, and the warning either appears in the run or it does not.

Closes #65

# Is production ready to be deployed to? Reads only — creates nothing, changes nothing,
# safe to run any number of times.
#
# Run it while working through the provisioning checklist (issue #27) to see what is
# still missing, and run it first when a deploy fails, because most deploy failures are
# a resource or a secret that is not there.
name: preflight

on:
  workflow_dispatch:
    inputs:
      stage:
        description: 'Which checks to run'
        type: choice
        default: all
        options: [all, resources, serving]

jobs:
  preflight:
    name: does production exist
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
